what: Browsers offer three small stores: localStorage (kept until cleared), sessionStorage (one tab) and cookies (sent to the server with requests). Pick by what the data is: preferences in Web Storage, login sessions in a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie.
like: Like three places to keep notes: a drawer at home (localStorage), a sticky note on your desk that is binned when you leave (sessionStorage), and a hall pass the guard checks at every door (cookie).
why: Remember preferences and drafts without a server round trip
Keep login sessions out of reach of injected scripts
Avoid sending extra bytes with every request

steps.d: Key-value strings that survive restarts, shared by all same-origin tabs. Good for theme or a dismissed banner. It is synchronous, so keep it small.
Cleared when the tab closes and separate in each tab. Good for a multi-step form draft.
The server sets Set-Cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite. The browser then sends it on matching requests without your code touching it.
An injected script can read anything in Web Storage but cannot read an HttpOnly cookie, which is why session ids belong there.
A storage event fires in other same-origin tabs when localStorage changes, a cheap way to sync logout or theme.

numbers.l: Web Storage limit per origin for each of localStorage and sessionStorage
usual cap on a single cookie, and cookies ride on every matching request
SameSite value browsers assume when none is set
Safari may delete script-created storage after 7 days of use without interaction (server-set cookies are exempt)

choices.d: Preferences: localStorage. Per-tab drafts: sessionStorage. Session id: HttpOnly cookie. Large or structured data: IndexedDB.
HttpOnly blocks script access, Secure sends only over HTTPS, SameSite limits cross-site sending (None needs Secure). The __Host- prefix forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain.
Max-Age beats Expires and does not depend on the client clock. A cookie with neither is a session cookie, deleted when the browser session ends.
Cookies are sent with every matching request, so keep them small; MDN advises against using them for client-side storage.

instead.why: For large or structured data, with asynchronous access that does not block the page
For the full login design: cookies, tokens, refresh and CSRF

breaks.d: A JWT or session id kept in localStorage is readable by any injected script.
breaks.see: Account takeover after a single XSS bug
breaks.fix: Session in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, plus CSP to reduce XSS

breaks.d: Writes throw QuotaExceededError, or storage is unavailable in some privacy modes.
breaks.fix: Wrap every access in try/catch and run fine without storage

breaks.d: SameSite=None without Secure is rejected, and browsers increasingly block third-party cookies.
breaks.see: Embedded widget or SSO loses its session
breaks.fix: Design for first-party cookies; set SameSite=None; Secure only where truly needed

say: I match data to storage: preferences in localStorage, per-tab state in sessionStorage, and the session in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.
I never keep session tokens in Web Storage because any XSS can read them; OWASP says the same.
I wrap storage in try/catch and keep it small, since it is synchronous and capped at about 5 MiB.

followups.a: The cookie is sent on same-site requests and on top-level navigations from other sites, but not on cross-site subrequests. It is the default when SameSite is unset.

followups.q: How do two tabs stay in sync?
followups.a: The storage event fires in other same-origin tabs when localStorage changes. It does not fire in the tab that made the change.

followups.q: Can JavaScript delete an HttpOnly cookie?
followups.a: It cannot read it, and the server normally clears it by resending the cookie with Max-Age=0 on the same name, path and domain.

today: Browsers keep tightening cookies: SameSite defaults to Lax and third-party cookies are increasingly blocked. Current guidance is to keep sessions in HttpOnly cookies, keep Web Storage for non-sensitive preferences, and move anything large to IndexedDB.

check.q: Where should a session id live?
check.why: Scripts cannot read HttpOnly cookies, so XSS cannot copy the session.

check.q: You change localStorage in tab A. Where does the storage event fire?
check.a: In other same-origin tabs, not tab A
check.why: It lets other tabs react to changes.

check.q: Which SameSite value is assumed when none is set?
check.why: Browsers treat a missing SameSite as Lax.

sources.t: MDN: Storage quotas and eviction criteria
